stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the record of the Sacco and Vanzetti case: In 1920, Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti, two Italian immigrants and anarchists, were arrested in Massachusetts and charged with robbing a shoe-factory payroll and killing two men. They were convicted in 1921. Many observers questioned whether the trial had been fair, pointing to the judge's conduct and the men's radical politics. After six years of appeals, both men were executed in August 1927.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the case record as summarized in 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 22.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from the Sacco and Vanzetti case record as summarized in 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 22
stem: Critics of the trial argued that the verdict rested more on the men's background than on the evidence because

options.text: the jury had never heard any witnesses
options.misconception: The trial lasted weeks and heard many witnesses. The critics' complaint was about how the evidence was weighed, not its absence.

options.text: the men had confessed to the crime
options.misconception: Both men maintained their innocence to the end. No confession existed for the critics to point to.

options.text: the judge had freed both men at once
options.misconception: The judge did not free them. They stayed in prison through six years of appeals and were executed in 1927.

options.text: their anarchist views marked them as dangerous men

rationales.A: The trial lasted weeks and heard many witnesses. The critics' complaint was about how the evidence was weighed, not its absence.
rationales.B: Both men maintained their innocence to the end. No confession existed for the critics to point to.
rationales.C: The judge did not free them. They stayed in prison through six years of appeals and were executed in 1927.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the judge's conduct and the men's radical politics were at the center of the doubts. In the Red Scare years, being an immigrant anarchist was itself treated as proof of danger.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the critics questioned: whether the trial had been fair.
2. Ask what they pointed to: the judge's conduct and the men's radical politics.
3. Ask what that means: the men's identity, not the facts of the robbery, drove the verdict.
4. Name the charge. Background: in the Red Scare years, being an immigrant anarchist was itself treated as proof of danger.
Remember: a fair-trial question is about what the verdict rested on, so check the evidence against the identity.
